title: Quality expectations, acceptance criteria and specifications
blurb: Define user's quality expectations, acceptance criteria, quality specifications, requirements and quality tolerance, and tell them apart from outcomes.
question: Which term describes a prioritized list of measurable criteria the project product must meet before the user will accept it?

teach.h: Three terms that build on each other
teach.body: Formally: user's quality expectations are a statement about the quality expected from the project product; acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of criteria it must meet before the user will accept it; quality specifications describe the quality measures used in quality control and the levels a finished product must meet. In plain English: what users hope for, how they will decide to say yes, and the exact measures each product is checked against.

teach.h: From broad hopes to exact measures
teach.caption: Each level gets more precise. The first two sit in the project product description; specifications sit in product descriptions.

head: Term
What it is
Where it lives
rows: Statement of quality expected from the project product
Prioritized, measurable list the user's acceptance depends on
Measures used in quality control and levels to meet
A need or expectation documented in an approved product
Permissible deviation in quality before escalation

teach.body: A requirement is a need or expectation that has been documented in an approved management product, so an idea mentioned in a corridor is not yet a requirement. Quality tolerance is the permissible deviation in a product's quality before it must be escalated to the next level of management. Tolerances are set using the prioritized acceptance criteria and the quality specifications.

teach.caption: Inside the band the team carries on; below it, the deviation is escalated.

teach.h: Outcomes and benefits are not quality expectations
teach.body: Quality expectations describe the project PRODUCT. 'Customers will trust our brand more' or 'donations will rise' describe what happens after the product is used: an outcome (a result of change) or a benefit (a measurable improvement). They belong to the business case, not the project product description. Exam stems often dress an outcome up as a quality expectation.

teach.h: Which kind of statement is it?

root.label: Does it describe the product itself?

children.edge: No: a result of using it
children.label: Outcome or benefit

teach.body: Brackenford Homes is building an online portal for tenants. Senior user Mariam Begum says it must be 'easy for older tenants to use': a user's quality expectation. Project manager Callum Reid turns this into acceptance criteria, ranked by priority: a repair can be reported in five steps or fewer, and the site passes the agreed accessibility standard. The product description for the repair form adds specifications such as field labels readable at 200% zoom. 'Fewer complaint calls' is noted as a benefit for the business case.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) An outcome or a benefit ('improved reputation', 'more donations') is NOT a user's quality expectation or an acceptance criterion. (2) Acceptance criteria are prioritized and measurable; expectations are broad. (3) Quality specifications are written per product in product descriptions, not in the project product description.

items: User's quality expectations: broad statement of quality expected from the project product (PPD).
Acceptance criteria: prioritized, measurable list for user acceptance (PPD).
Quality specifications: measures and levels used in quality control (product descriptions).
Requirement: a need or expectation documented in an approved management product.
Quality tolerance: permissible deviation before escalation, set from criteria and specifications.

summary: You can now define user's quality expectations, acceptance criteria, quality specifications, requirements and quality tolerance, and say where each is recorded. You can also spot an outcome or benefit disguised as a quality expectation.

A.q: Which term describes a prioritized list of criteria that the project product must meet before the user will accept it?
A.why: Acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of criteria the project product must meet before the user will accept it (manual 8.1.1).

whyNot.0: Quality specifications are the measures and levels applied to each product in quality control.
whyNot.1: User's quality expectations are a broad statement of the quality expected from the project product.
whyNot.3: Quality tolerance is the permissible deviation in a product's quality before escalation.

A.q: Where are the user's quality expectations captured?
A.why: The user's quality expectations are a statement about the quality expected from the project product, captured in the project product description.

whyNot.1: The quality register records quality activities and their results.
whyNot.2: Work package descriptions pass work to teams; they reference product descriptions.
whyNot.3: The end stage report reviews stage performance.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A [?] is a need or expectation that is documented in an approved management product.
A.why: A requirement is a need or expectation documented in an approved management product (manual 8.1.1).

whyNot.0: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome.
whyNot.2: A quality specification describes measures and levels used in quality control.
whyNot.3: Acceptance criteria are the prioritized list the user's acceptance depends on.

B.q: A charity's senior user says the new website should 'increase public trust in the charity'. How should this statement be classified?
options: As a user's quality expectation for the website
As an acceptance criterion for the website
As a quality specification in a product description
As an outcome, not a quality expectation
B.why: Increased trust is a result of change after the website is used: an outcome, not a statement about the quality of the product itself.

whyNot.0: A quality expectation describes the quality of the project product, not the result of using it.
whyNot.1: Acceptance criteria are measurable attributes of the product, not the effect of the product.
whyNot.2: Quality specifications are product measures used in quality control.

options: The range of cost within which quality checks may be carried out
The number of failed quality checks allowed in a single stage
The level of quality agreed by the senior supplier for each product
The permissible deviation in a product's quality before escalation
B.why: Quality tolerance is the permissible deviation in a product's quality allowed before it must be escalated to the next level of management (manual 8.2.1.2).

whyNot.0: Cost tolerance concerns spend, not variation in product quality.
whyNot.1: Tolerance is about deviation from quality criteria, not a count of failed checks.
whyNot.2: Quality levels come from users' requirements; tolerance is the allowed deviation from them.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Quality specifications are recorded in product descriptions.
2. Acceptance criteria are recorded in the quality register.
3. Acceptance criteria are prioritized and measurable.
4. User's quality expectations are written for each product.
B.why: Quality specifications sit in product descriptions (1), and acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of measurable criteria (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: acceptance criteria are in the project product description.
whyNot.1: Both are false: acceptance criteria are in the PPD, and expectations are a project-level statement.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: user's quality expectations are about the project product as a whole.

C.q: Which management product holds the acceptance criteria, and which holds the quality specifications for a single product?
C.why: Acceptance criteria are in the project product description; each product's quality specifications are in its product description.

whyNot.2: The QMA describes techniques, standards and responsibilities; the register records activities.
whyNot.3: The project brief is assembled in starting up a project, and a work package description passes work to a team; neither is where these terms are defined.

C.q: What are quality tolerances set from?
options: The business's risk appetite and the project's risk budget
Prioritized acceptance criteria and quality specifications
The cost and time tolerances already set in the stage plan
The results already recorded in the quality register
C.why: Prioritized acceptance criteria and quality specifications are used to set quality tolerances.

whyNot.0: Risk appetite and budget inform risk tolerance and responses.
whyNot.2: Cost and time tolerances are separate aspects of performance.
whyNot.3: The register records results against the tolerances; it does not set them.

C.q: Which statement is a quality specification rather than a user's quality expectation?
options: The guide should feel welcoming to new visitors
The service should be reliable for staff
Each printed map must be accurate to within 2 metres
Visitors should find the trail enjoyable
C.why: A quality specification gives a measure and a level a product must meet, which quality control can check.

whyNot.0: This is a broad, unmeasured statement typical of a user's quality expectation.
whyNot.1: Reliability stated without a measure is a high-level expectation.
whyNot.3: Enjoyment is a broad expectation and close to an outcome, with no measure to check.

reteach.title: Ordering a new kitchen
reteach.question: How do you get from 'I want a nice kitchen' to something a fitter can check?

blocks.body: 'I want a bright, practical kitchen' is your quality expectation. 'I will only accept it if the worktop is 3 metres, the units are white and it is finished by June' are your acceptance criteria, ranked so the fitter knows what matters most. The spec sheet for each cupboard (hinge type, door gap of 3 mm, plus or minus 1 mm) holds the quality specifications and tolerance. 'Friends will admire it' is an outcome, not a requirement of the kitchen.

blocks.text: Admiring friends are a result of the kitchen, not a quality of the kitchen.

explain.body: A broad statement about the quality expected from the project product, captured in the project product description.

test.q: Which statement about user's quality expectations is correct?
options: They are recorded separately in each product description
They are a statement about the project product's quality
They list the results of quality checks
They are set by the senior supplier
test.why: User's quality expectations are a statement about the quality expected from the project product, captured in the PPD.

whyNot.0: Product descriptions hold quality specifications for individual products.
whyNot.2: Results of checks are recorded in the quality register.
whyNot.3: Expectations come from the users, represented by the senior user.

explain.body: A prioritized list of measurable criteria the project product must meet before the user will accept it; also in the PPD.

test.q: What makes acceptance criteria different from user's quality expectations?
options: They are written by the team manager
They are kept in the quality register
test.why: Acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of measurable criteria; expectations are a broader statement.

whyNot.1: Criteria are agreed with the users; the team manager produces products to meet them.
whyNot.2: Acceptance criteria are in the project product description.

explain.body: The measures applied by those doing quality control and the levels a finished product must meet, written in each product description.

options: The business layer when setting tolerances
test.why: Quality specifications describe the measures applied by those performing quality control and the levels to be met.

whyNot.0: The business layer sets project tolerances; specifications are applied in quality control.
whyNot.2: Funding decisions rest on the business case.
whyNot.3: Planning stages is the project manager's work; specifications guide checking.

explain.body: If a statement describes what happens after the product is used, it is an outcome or benefit for the business case.

test.q: A sponsor lists 'more visitors to the museum' as a quality expectation for a new gallery. What is it?
test.why: More visitors is a result of the gallery being used, so it is an outcome or benefit, not a statement of the product's quality.

whyNot.0: Acceptance criteria describe measurable attributes of the product.
whyNot.1: A specification is a product measure checked in quality control.
whyNot.2: Quality tolerance is the allowed deviation in a product's quality.
